paras: The near-lynching of Lock Johnson took place in Sweet Springs, Missouri, in early November 1888, when Johnson, a Black man accused of stabbing a young man of the town, was captured by a posse and "narrowly escaped" lynching. Johnson was not killed, and the episode is known from a single paragraph in the Lexington Intelligencer.

According to a Sweet Springs dispatch dated November 7, a young man, a son of Eli Smith who lived east of town, was "repeatedly stabbed" by a man the paper's OCR text renders as "Lock EFT johnson, a negro." Johnson fled but was captured by a posse led by City Marshal Beatty, W. T. Hall and others. The dispatch said he "narrowly escaped" lynching, without saying who sought to lynch him, how many there were, or how the lynching was prevented. Smith's injuries, it added, would "probably result fatally."
No report of Johnson's jailing, an indictment, a trial, or Smith's death appears in the coverage.

The Intelligencer of Lexington, Missouri, printed the item on November 10 among local paragraphs on its first page, directly after a report from the same correspondent that John Cain, "colored," had been shot dead at nearby Blackburn by Dave Hancock, "white," after a political discussion. The paper identified Johnson by race, named the marshal and another member of the posse that captured him, and reported the near-lynching in one clause without comment. No other report of the episode was found.

bases: The only report says Johnson, accused of stabbing a man, was captured by a posse and 'narrowly escaped' lynching, an averted mob killing (A1).

No one was killed: Johnson is reported only to have narrowly escaped lynching after his capture (A1). The paragraph does not say who tried or wanted to lynch him or how many, so the episode is at most an averted lynching.
One paragraph in one paper, a Sweet Springs item in the Lexington Intelligencer (A1), with no second report found.

accounts.gist: Johnson repeatedly stabbed Smith's son, fled, was captured by Marshal Beatty's posse, and narrowly escaped lynching; Smith was expected to die.

framing.detail: A dated news paragraph among local items, calling Johnson 'a negro' and reporting the near-lynching without comment.

Black: the paragraph calls him 'a negro'.

The paper names no county; only the town, Sweet Springs, Mo.
The posse (led by City Marshal Beatty) captured him; who threatened to lynch him is not said.
